The Japanese clawed salamander Onychodactylus japonicus is a stream-breeding amphibian endemic to the mountainous regions of Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu. Embryos develop within a gelatinous egg mass, and eclosion from the jelly capsule occurs after an incubation period of approximately 148 days [ab = approximately 148 days] when maintained at a constant water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Upon emergence, the neonates are relatively well-developed compared to many other hynobiid species, with a total length at birth measuring 2.6 cm [Lb = 2.6 cm]. These recently hatched larvae, weighing approximately 0.0654 g [Wwb = approximately 0.0654 g]rams, are lecithotrophic for a brief period before transitioning to exogenous feeding. This relatively long incubation, characteristic of montane salamanders, likely reflects the thermal constraints of their cool, headwater stream habitats.

Following the onset of exogenous feeding, the aquatic tadpoles enter a prolonged larval phase that can last for several years under typical stream conditions. At a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is estimated to be 5 years , a remarkably extended larval period that distinguishes this species from many other Japanese salamanders. During this time, the free-swimming larva grows steadily, and the transition to a terrestrial juvenile is marked by the resorption of gills and tail fin. At the metamorphic climax, the total length at metamorphosis is approximately 8 cm , a size that reflects the substantial investment in larval growth. This lengthy larval duration is thought to be an adaptation to the unproductive, cold-water environments where these salamanders are found, allowing them to accumulate sufficient energy reserves.

Upon completing metamorphosis, the post-metamorphic juvenile continues to grow for several more years before attaining sexual maturation. The total length at puberty is estimated to be 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], a value inferred from comparisons with related species such as Hynobius nebulosus. The maximum recorded total length for this species, or ultimate total length, reaches 17 cm [Li = 17 cm], placing it among the larger members of the genus. The fully grown adults, weighing up to 9.65 g [Wwi = up to 9.65 g]rams, are adapted for a semi-terrestrial existence but remain closely associated with the cool, rocky streams where they breed. The overall slow growth and late maturity are consistent with a life-history strategy tuned to low metabolic rates and stable, nutrient-poor environments.

Reproductive output in this species is modest, reflecting the energetic constraints of a cold-water lifestyle. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females have been observed to produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], with each clutch containing just a single egg [N_R_i = each clutch containing just a single egg]. This very low fecundity, resulting in just one egg per year, is unusual among amphibians and underscores the species' extremely conservative reproductive strategy. The maximum reproductive rate, achieved only under optimal conditions, is thus limited to the production of one offspring per year. Such a slow pace of reproduction necessitates a relatively long adult lifespan to ensure population stability and replacement.

Longevity data for Onychodactylus japonicus indicate a potential lifespan of over 14 years under natural conditions. The maximum lifespan is estimated to be 14.2 years [am = 14.2 years] when measured at a stable temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a duration that is considerable for an amphibian of its body size. This extended lifespan is a critical component of the species' life-history strategy, compensating for its exceptionally low annual reproductive output by allowing individuals multiple breeding opportunities across many seasons. The combination of late maturity, protracted larval development, minimal fecundity, and long adult survival paints a picture of a species adapted to a highly stable but resource-limited environment, where the risk of juvenile mortality is high and reproductive investment must be spread across many years to be successful.
